source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-correction that looks good with oracle labels vanishes when the label is removed. The earlier gains came from using the ground-truth answer to decide when to stop.
numbers: With oracle labels (Table 2): GPT-3.5 HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-4: 29.0 to 59.0 as extracted). Without oracle (Table 3): GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0; Llama-2-70B GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 to 36.5.
quote: Our findings indicate that LLMs struggle to self-correct their reasoning in this setting.
limits: Table 2 text extraction is scrambled, so oracle-row cell assignment is approximate; the no-oracle numbers (Tables 3-4) are clear. 200 sampled questions per dataset for non-GPT-3.5 models (100 for HotpotQA); max two rounds.
agent_relevance: G2 holds: a revise step triggered by the model's own doubt lowers accuracy. Only code-found failure signals justify revision.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) - direction of change
finding: After two self-correction rounds the model flips correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse. GPT-3.5 on GSM8K keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time. On CommonSenseQA the prompt biases it to switch options.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 74.7% no change; correct-to-incorrect exceeds incorrect-to-correct. Different feedback prompts on GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K: 88.0-91.0 vs 91.5 baseline; CSQA 74.5-83.5 vs 84.0. Llama-2 CSQA: 24.0-43.0 vs 64.0 baseline.
limits: Exact flip percentages are in Figure 1, which did not extract cleanly. Stronger models (GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo) mostly keep answers, so they lose less.
agent_relevance: Asking 'are you sure?' with no evidence is a perturbation, not a check. The schema should never run a blanket critique pass (supports G1).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) - debate vs self-consistency
finding: Multi-agent debate gains are a vote effect, not a critique effect. At equal response count, plain self-consistency beats debate.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: standard 76.7 (1 response); self-consistency 82.5 (3), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9); debate 83.2 (3 responses, round 1) and 83.0 (9 responses, round 2).
limits: Table 7 extraction jumbled; response counts assigned by reading order. Debate used 3 agents, 2 rounds.
agent_relevance: Spend budget on independent samples chosen by code, not on inter-sample critique (G5).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) - prompt confound
finding: Some published Self-Refine gains come from a weak first prompt. Putting the requirement in the first prompt beats self-correction, and re-applying self-correction then lowers the score again.
numbers: CommonGen-Hard concept coverage: Madaan standard 44.0 to self-correct 67.0 (7 calls); Huang improved standard prompt 81.8 to self-correct 75.1.
limits: Single task and one model (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613).
agent_relevance: Put every checkable requirement in the first prompt before adding any revision loop.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Splitting self-correction in two shows the weak half is finding the error, not fixing it. On BIG-Bench Mistake the best models locate the first wrong step poorly.
numbers: Overall mistake-location accuracy, GPT-4: 39.80 (direct trace), 52.87 (direct step), 43.40 (CoT step); GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.44/14.78/14.31; PaLM 2 Unicorn 17.09/23.67/24.65. 5 tasks, 300 traces each mostly; traces about 85% incorrect.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Traces are mostly wrong by design (skewed dataset). Per-step prompting lowers accuracy on traces that have no mistake. Weighted F1 for the correctness label is near an all-wrong baseline of 78.
agent_relevance: Locate the error with code (tests, checker output, line numbers) and give that location to the model. Do not ask the model to find it.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) - backtracking with oracle location
finding: With the true mistake location, backtracking (regenerate that step and continue) helps more than it hurts. A random location gives much smaller gains, so it is not just resampling.
numbers: Word sorting: 11.11% of originally right traces turned wrong, 23.53% of originally wrong traces turned right. Other deltas for correct/incorrect sets: -11.43/+36.86, -13.33/+21.57, -6.82/+18.06. With a simulated classifier, losses flatten at about 65% mistake-finding accuracy.
limits: Only PaLM 2 Unicorn as generator; small correct-trace sets (45 per task). Net gain depends on base accuracy: base 50% gives 68.6%, base 99% gives 92.8% (their worked example).
agent_relevance: Correction is cheap once the failing step is known. Needs a locator of roughly 65% accuracy or better, which tests can supply and the model cannot.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) - trained locator transfer
finding: A small fine-tuned PaLM 2 Otter locator trained on four tasks improved mistake finding on the held-out fifth task in 4 of 5 cases, but stayed below the accuracy needed for reliable backtracking.
numbers: Held-out differences vs 3-shot Unicorn range from -0.67 to +22.59 points (Table 7); classifier accuracies 6.00-37.67.
limits: Row-to-task alignment in the extracted table is uncertain. Classifier accuracies are below the 65% threshold.
agent_relevance: Learned error locators are not ready; deterministic checks remain the reliable route.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (TACL)
finding: Survey of self-correction papers up to May 2024. No prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted LLM feedback alone, except on tasks where checking is exceptionally easy. Reliable external feedback and large-scale fine-tuning do work.
numbers: Three research questions: RQ1 intrinsic self-correction of best-possible initial responses; RQ2 with external information; RQ3 versus strong baselines. Table 4 flags oracle stopping (RCI, Reflexion) and weak first prompts (Self-Refine, CAI) as over-evaluation.
quote: The bottleneck is in feedback generation.
limits: Survey covers work through May 2024; later RL-trained models are only briefly noted (section 12).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2/S5: revise from tool output; treat prompted self-feedback as unproven. Also gives a fairness checklist for our own measurements.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) survey - task properties
finding: Intrinsic self-correction works when verifying is much easier than producing, for example when the answer can be split into independent items (CoVe style list answers). The hypothesis 'recognising errors is easier than avoiding them' only holds for such tasks.
numbers: No pooled numeric effect; qualitative classification across dozens of studies. Strong baselines named: self-consistency, pass@k, generate-and-rank.
limits: Qualitative synthesis, no meta-analytic effect size.
agent_relevance: Route to self-correction only for decomposable outputs or when a tool can check. Always compare to equal-budget sampling (G5).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) Evaluating LLMs at Detecting Errors in LLM Responses (ReaLMistake, COLM 2024)
finding: Twelve LLMs detect objective, expert-annotated errors in GPT-4 and Llama 2 70B outputs at low recall. All do worse than humans. Self-consistency, multi-model majority vote and evaluation-step hints did not help.
numbers: Human inter-annotator binary error F1 95.7. 14 expert annotators, 90 hours, 3 tasks, 4 error categories. Stronger models (higher LMSYS Elo) get higher precision but lower recall. Several detectors score below a random baseline in F1.
limits: Per-model recall/precision table did not extract cleanly. Detector prompts are zero-shot; sensitivity to small prompt changes was large.
agent_relevance: A model-as-checker misses most real errors. Do not treat 'the critic found nothing' as a pass (G3).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: Self-Refine helps most on style, preference and constraint-coverage tasks. It does almost nothing on math, because the model cannot tell whether the answer is wrong.
numbers: GPT-4: sentiment reversal 3.8 to 36.2, code readability 15.0 to 45.0; GPT-3.5 acronym generation 41.6 to 56.4; math reasoning (GPT-3.5) 64.1 to 64.1 (0 change). ChatGPT said 'everything looks good' on 94% of math instances. Claimed 20% absolute average gain.
quote: a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs to think that 'everything looks good'
limits: Humans or GPT-4 judged several tasks; 82/68/71% metric-human correlation. Huang et al. later showed the constrained-generation gain is partly a prompt artifact.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback works where there is a clear surface criterion and fails on silent logic errors.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine - ablations and failure analysis
finding: Specific feedback beats generic feedback, and no feedback is worst. In failures, the feedback was the problem, not the rewrite.
numbers: Code optimization 27.5 (specific) vs 26.0 (generic) vs 24.8 (none); sentiment 43.2 vs 31.2 vs 0; acronym 56.4 vs 54.0 vs 48.0. Of failed cases, 33% wrong error location, 61% wrong fix suggested, 6% bad execution of good feedback. With an external math-error signal gains rose by 5%+. Vicuna-13B could not follow the feedback format.
limits: 70 manually analysed samples (35 success, 35 failure). Small models may not support the loop.
agent_relevance: Concrete failing output as feedback is the part that matters (G2). Small base models may need a stronger fixer.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: iterative prompting for reasoning
finding: On graph colouring, GPT-4 self-critique does not beat a single attempt. GPT-4 is a poor verifier: it rejects almost every colouring, including correct ones. With a sound external verifier success rises to about 40%, but the detail of the feedback does not matter.
numbers: Baseline 16%. Verifying: of 100 optimal colourings only 2 accepted; of 500 colourings (118 correct) it called 30 correct and was right 5 times. In 40 runs where the generator produced an optimal colouring, the LLM verifier recognised it in 0 (39 hallucinated a violation). Only 4 of 100 runs were stopped by the LLM verifier, none correct. Sound verifier: binary, first-error and all-errors feedback all about 40%; 15 independent samples at t=1.0 also about 40%.
quote: blindfolded guessing does just as well as careful, crafted feedback.
limits: One task (graph colouring, 100 instances), GPT-4 only; local fixes were applied 84-98% of the time, even for false ('evil') errors (94% fixed).
agent_relevance: The gain comes from more tries plus a trusted filter. Spend budget on samples checked by code, not on richer critique text.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: In Blocksworld planning, LLM verifier output gives a small gain over one attempt but far below a sound verifier. The LLM verifier has a large false-positive rate.
numbers: Plan accuracy: generator alone 40/100; LLM+LLM backprompting 55/100 (3.48 iterations); LLM+VAL 88/100. LLM verifier accuracy 61/100 with 38 false positives out of 45 invalid plans (84%); 54 of 55 valid plans accepted. With VAL: binary only 37/50 vs first-error 43/50 vs all-errors 43/50.
limits: 100 instances, one domain, GPT-4 at temperature 0. The abstract says self-critique diminishes performance, but its Table 1 shows 40 to 55, so the small gain may be mostly extra tries.
agent_relevance: False 'valid' verdicts end the loop early. Never let model judgement stop the loop (G1, G3).

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot (COLM 2026)
finding: Models correct an error when it is shown as the user's, but not when the same error sits in their own previous turn. This activation failure is a training artefact, not missing knowledge.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average 64.5% blind spot. Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. BIG-Bench Mistake tasks: 62.8%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces cut the blind spot 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cut it 89.3%. Reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot.
quote: Wait requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Injected errors, so 64.5% is a property of the design, not a rate of real-world failure. Mechanistic work only on Llama and Qwen at 7-8B.
agent_relevance: Present the earlier attempt as someone else's work and use a role flip or a 'Wait' cue when a check has failed. Do not ask the same context to audit itself (G4).

source: Tsui (2026) - Wait vs reasoning models
finding: Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model nearly matches its reasoning-trained sibling on the self-correction benchmark.
limits: Benchmark uses injected, shown errors; it measures activation, not discovery of unseen errors.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-triggered cue after a failed check is worth testing at S5.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via RL (SCoRe)
finding: Prompted and SFT self-correction on MATH makes the second try worse or flat. Multi-turn RL on self-generated data gives the first clearly positive intrinsic self-correction gain.
numbers: MATH (Gemini 1.5 Flash): base 52.6 to 41.4 (-11.2); Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8 (-1.0); STaR 53.6 to 54.0 (+0.4); Pair-SFT 52.4 to 54.2 (+1.8); SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4). HumanEval (Gemini 1.0 Pro): Self-Refine -1.2, Pair-SFT -1.8, SCoRe +12.2 (52.4 to 64.6).
limits: Needs training, so not available to a scaffold. Single run per method; greedy decoding. Failure modes: distribution shift and behaviour collapse into never editing.
agent_relevance: Shows the capability can be trained; for a scaffold-only agent the same-model second try stays risky unless a check gates it.

source: Qu et al. (2024) Recursive Introspection (RISE)
finding: Fine-tuning on multi-turn correction rollouts lets small models improve over five turns on math. Prompted Self-Refine degrades results.
numbers: MATH: Mistral-7B 6.7 to 29.7 (+22.4) after five turns with oracle early stop; GSM8K Mistral-7B 35.3 to 68.6 (+33.3) with oracle. GPT-3.5 itself gains only 4.6% over five turns; Self-Refine degrades results across the board.
limits: Several headline numbers use oracle early termination. Trained models, small benchmark set.
agent_relevance: With a model-judged stop, gains are small; with a verified stop they are large.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (ICLR 2024)
finding: Tool feedback (search, code interpreter) drives the gain. Removing the tool gives gains near zero or negative on some tasks.
numbers: text-davinci-003 GSM8K: PoT 70.1, CRITIC w/o tool 68.3 (-1.8). ChatGPT GSM8K: PoT 72.5, CRITIC w/o tool 78.2 (+5.7), CRITIC with tool 77.0 (+4.5). text-davinci AmbigNQ F1: CoT 58.6, w/o tool 58.3, CRITIC 64.9.
limits: Table rows extracted with some ambiguity, and the ChatGPT GSM8K ablation shows a gain without the tool, so the ablation is mixed. Oracle variants correct only wrong answers.
agent_relevance: Evidence that external, tool-found failure signals are the useful part (G2); results differ by model and task.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: With compute counted, self-repair of code gives small and uneven gains over drawing more independent samples. The bottleneck is the model's feedback on its own code.
numbers: On APPS GPT-4 beat baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 gains marginal except at the largest first-sample count; harder problems gave up to a 34% relative gain for GPT-3.5. Repair success with human feedback 52.60% vs GPT-4 self-feedback 33.30% (introductory 62.21 vs 42.64; interview 45.67 vs 19.33; competition 14.67 vs 3.67).
limits: Unit tests defined failure; 16 human participants, 40 failing programs, 2 human notes per program. HumanEval near ceiling.
agent_relevance: Feedback quality caps the gain. Diverse first attempts beat deep repair of one attempt, matching G4.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction (ACL 2025)
finding: Intrinsic self-correction makes models waver. Even on simple yes/no questions it changes right answers, and reasoning models show human-like failures (overthinking, cognitive overload, perfectionism).
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of answers more than 6 times in a 10-round chat. Llama-3-8B changes its internal answer 14.1% of the time in self-correction vs 8.3% in first generation. o1-mini wrote 'think' 15.4 times in failed runs vs 5.3 in normal runs. Mitigations: repeating the question after feedback, and SFT on a few samples.
limits: Table cells extracted poorly, so per-model accuracy drops are not quoted. Four tasks (yes/no QA, decision making, reasoning, programming).
agent_relevance: Repeat the original task after any feedback, and cap rounds (G1).

source: Song et al. (2025) Mind the Gap: Examining the Self-Improvement Capabilities of LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Self-improvement depends on the generation-verification gap. The relative gap rises linearly with log pre-training compute for some verifiers, but not for all, and iterative self-improvement saturates in a few rounds.
numbers: Relative gap grows with log pre-training FLOPs (CoT-score verification), the absolute gap does not. Saturation within 2-3 rounds independent of model size. Generalised 4x4 Sudoku: most models fail to self-improve though checking is easy; only the largest Qwen-2 72B improved.
limits: Scaling holds only for certain verification methods; chain-of-thought verification was more stable than multiple-choice.
agent_relevance: Self-verification cannot be assumed for any task. Measure the gap on our task before trusting a model check.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (COLM 2025), on DeepSeek-R1 aha moment
finding: R1-Zero reported an 'aha moment' of self-reflection learned by RL. This paper and prior replications show base models already produce reflection words, and reflection frequency does not track accuracy.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3-Base, run on 500 MATH questions with the R1 template, produces self-reflections including 'Aha' and 'wait'. R1-Zero reflects more often, but reflection behaviour is not positively correlated with higher accuracy.
limits: Keyword counts are a weak proxy for real error correction.
agent_relevance: Do not count 'wait' tokens as evidence of correction. Score by checks that pass.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Automatically Correcting LLMs: surveying diverse self-correction strategies (TACL 2024)
finding: Survey used as background by Huang and Kamoi: separates training-time, generation-time and post-hoc correction and internal versus external feedback.
numbers: No pooled numbers.
limits: PDF did not download cleanly in this session; not read, so marked unopened.
agent_relevance: Taxonomy only; no added measured result.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: On 3,400 expert-annotated competition and Olympiad math solutions, models must name the earliest wrong step. Reasoning-trained models find errors far better than ordinary chat models, and prompted general models beat most process reward models.
numbers: Overall F1: o1-mini 87.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5, GPT-4o-0806 61.9. Existing PRMs fall behind on harder sets beyond GSM8K and MATH; a Qwen2.5-Math-7B PRM trained on PRM800K reached 68.2 / 62.6 / 50.7 on the first three subsets.
limits: Math only; critic prompts step by step; per-model cells for other models were not cleanly extractable from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Error finding improves with reasoning training, so a reasoning-tuned model may serve as a locator, but test it against code checks first (G2).
